# 28. Client Handoff & Documentation

<!-- Generated by tools/build_checklists.py. Edit the generator to change checklist structure. -->

**Purpose:** Leave the client with clear ownership, maintenance rules, credentials guidance, and enough documentation to operate the static site safely.

## Universal Constraints
- [ ] The solution must remain static front-end only: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, documents, and generated static files only.
- [ ] The stack must avoid proprietary lock-in, paid builders, paid plugins, closed hosting features that cannot be replaced, and opaque third-party scripts where an open or free-tier-friendly alternative exists.
- [ ] Every decision must be documented as a quality rule, acceptance criterion, or exception with rationale; implementation notes belong outside the checklist.
- [ ] Every checklist item must be testable by review, automated audit, source inspection, browser testing, or client sign-off.
- [ ] Manual exceptions must record the owner, reason, expiration date, affected pages, and residual risk.

## Must Exist
- [ ] A handoff document covering repository, hosting, DNS, analytics, forms, content workflow, assets, and support boundaries.
- [ ] A credentials inventory that records where access lives without storing passwords in the document.
- [ ] A maintenance schedule for content updates, dependency review, link checks, forms, analytics, backups, domain renewal, and legal review.
- [ ] A content editing guide for common updates such as hours, team, services, prices, portfolio, articles, and images.
- [ ] A launch artifact bundle with sitemap, QA report, accessibility notes, performance report, analytics plan, and legal review status.
- [ ] A rollback and emergency contact process.
- [ ] A license inventory for fonts, images, icons, code, and tools.
- [ ] A known limitations and future improvements list.

## Must Be True
- [ ] The client must control or have documented access to domain, hosting, repository, analytics, forms, and third-party accounts.
- [ ] Documentation must be specific to the delivered site, not generic boilerplate.
- [ ] The handoff must explain which parts are static and which external services process data.
- [ ] The client must know how to update critical business facts without breaking SEO or compliance.
- [ ] Maintenance tasks must have owners and cadence.
- [ ] No passwords, private keys, API secrets, or recovery codes may be stored in repository docs.
- [ ] Documentation must identify paid-risk items if any optional free tier could become paid at higher usage.
- [ ] The client must know how to request legal, accessibility, or content review when site behavior changes.

## Must Be Checked
- [ ] Check that all links in documentation work.
- [ ] Check that the repository can be cloned and understood by a new maintainer.
- [ ] Check that deployment instructions match the actual host.
- [ ] Check that generated files and source files are clearly distinguished.
- [ ] Check that analytics and form dashboards are accessible to the right owners.
- [ ] Check that domain renewal and DNS ownership are not dependent on the developer's personal account.
- [ ] Check that content update examples use real file paths and safe editing boundaries.
- [ ] Check that open issues are documented with risk and priority.

## Must Be Avoided
- [ ] Avoid handoff that assumes the client understands the build process.
- [ ] Avoid storing credentials in Markdown, spreadsheets, source files, or chat logs.
- [ ] Avoid leaving the client dependent on undocumented local scripts.
- [ ] Avoid hiding known defects or free-tier limits.
- [ ] Avoid handing over only design files without the actual static source.
- [ ] Avoid vague maintenance advice such as keep it updated without owner or schedule.

## Premium Acceptance Standard
- [ ] A competent maintainer must be able to operate the site from documentation alone.
- [ ] The client must leave with ownership clarity, not vendor dependency.
- [ ] Handoff must include quality evidence, not only files.
- [ ] Documentation must reduce future risk and support confident updates.

## Automation Hooks
- [ ] Use audit reports as handoff evidence.
- [ ] Use generated maintenance checklists and site config files to keep future audits repeatable.

## Detailed Best-Practice Review Areas
- [ ] Handoff documents purpose, audience, page list, sections, navigation, footer, CTAs, SEO, accessibility target, analytics plan, folder structure, asset naming, deployment, hosting, domain, DNS, forms, monitoring, and maintenance.
- [ ] Ownership is clear for repository, hosting, domain, DNS, forms, analytics, search tools, email, legal pages, updates, emergency fixes, backups, and future improvements.
- [ ] Another developer can edit pages, styles, scripts, assets, forms, metadata, redirects, analytics, deployment, troubleshooting, and rollback without proprietary tools.
- [ ] Client understands free/open-source constraints, static-site limits, what not to edit, how to publish safely, how to check forms/analytics, and how to request support.

## Report Output Required
- [ ] Report every failed automated check with severity, checklist category, issue code, affected file or page, evidence, whether it is script-fixable, and how to fix it.
- [ ] Report every manual-only failure with reviewer, affected page or component, expected standard, actual behavior, recommended fix, owner, and target date.
- [ ] Separate launch blockers from quality improvements so critical static-site failures cannot be hidden by low-priority polish notes.
- [ ] Attach the JSON audit report, Markdown audit report, screenshots where visual proof is needed, and manual QA evidence for browser, device, keyboard, screen reader, form, analytics, and live deployment checks.

## Evidence Required
- [ ] Record reviewed pages, tools used, dates, reviewers, unresolved exceptions, and links to generated reports.
- [ ] Attach screenshots or source references for failures that cannot be proven by automated reports.
- [ ] Mark checklist items as complete only when the production static output satisfies the rule.
